title: Ashtpadi 18, salok: the True Guru
hookLine: the salok honors the True Guru (Sukhmani 18)

lines: SOME NEVER HEAR WHAT THEY DID.
cards: A third-grade teacher catches a kid drawing in the margins and, instead of a scolding, hands over a sketchbook. A coach says one sentence at the right moment. A grandmother teaches bread and, without saying so, patience.
Some of those teachers never hear what they did. The word Sikh itself is about exactly this relationship. And the salok of the eighteenth ashtpadi is about the teacher at its center.

teach.b: The salok, in paraphrase: the one who knows the True Being is called the True Guru. In his company the Sikh is carried across; Nanak, sing the praises of the Lord. Start with one word in it: Sikh.
It's traced to a Sanskrit word for a student, a learner, a disciple. A Sikh, at root, is someone who is learning, not someone who has finished.
So every Sikh is defined by a relationship: you can't be a learner without a teacher. Then satgur, the True Guru. Notice how the salok defines it.

teach.h: SATGUR: THE ONE WHO KNOWS THE TRUE.
teach.b: Not by title, miracle or birth, but by knowing: the one who knows the True Being, sat purakh, is the True Guru. Sikhs understand the True Guru in more than one way, and hold these together.
God is the True Guru, the first and final teacher.
The ten Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, are honored as the True Guru, one light in ten lives.
And tradition says Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib itself, honored as the living Guru, and the community of the Khalsa is called the Guru Panth.
When the salok says in his company, Sikhs today hear the sangat gathered around the Guru Granth Sahib. Then the last phrase: sing the praises.
The response to a true teacher isn't admiring from a distance. It's singing: turning the gratitude outward, toward the One the teacher points to.
The next days follow that pattern: the Guru cares for the Sikh, the Sikh serves, and the line runs both ways.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the eighteenth ashtpadi with the salok on the True Guru; Sikhs honor God, the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as Guru, and gather as sangat in its presence.

games.q: the salok of the True Guru — tap the pairs.

s: the word Sikh comes from a word for a learner or disciple
a Sikh, at root, is someone still learning.
the salok defines the True Guru by miracles
by knowing: the one who knows the True Being is the True Guru.
Sikhs honor only one living human as Guru today

games.q: you've found a true teacher. by the eighteenth salok, what's the response?
o: admire the teacher from a distance.
sing the praises of the One the teacher points to.
become a teacher yourself right away.
games.why: the salok ends: Nanak, sing the praises of the Lord. gratitude to the teacher turns outward, toward the One.

practice: Bring to mind one teacher who taught you something true, a schoolteacher, a mentor, a parent, an author, and see their face, their handwriting, or the room where you learned.
Remember one specific thing they gave you, and thank them silently, in plain words. If you pray, thank the One they pointed you toward.

wordCard.voice: Satgur, the True Guru. The salok: the one who knows the True Being is the satgur, and in that company the Sikh, the learner, is carried across.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: satgur, the True Guru; sat, true, and gur, teacher.

carryVoice: Your line: thank the teacher. A Sikh, at root, is a learner, and no learner learns alone. See you tomorrow.
